========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Hello, yes, thank you for having me. Well, it’s... it’s a bit frustrating to even talk about because it sounds so silly at my age. I’m sixty years old, I’ve been a secondary school teacher for decades, so you’d think I’d know how to sit through a simple meeting by now, right? But that’s exactly what brought me in. I just... I keep getting up. 

It happens all the time in our faculty meetings, or even just at home at the dinner table when everyone else is perfectly content remaining seated. I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I just feel like I *have* to get up. I’ll convince myself I need to go refill my coffee—even if my mug is still half full—or I’ll pop up to check a stack of handouts on the side table, or sometimes I’ll just walk all the way to the back of the room and just stand there. 

And the thing is, none of it is ever really urgent. I mean, I could easily just stay in my chair like everybody else, but my brain finds these little excuses to leave my seat. Even at dinner, I'm constantly popping up to grab a salt shaker we don't really need, or to check on something in the kitchen. My husband just looks at me like, "Can you please just sit and eat?" and I'll look around and realize I'm the only one standing up again. It's just... I don't know, it's becoming very noticeable to the people around me, and honestly, to myself.

Well, distress... yes, I suppose it is. I mean, it’s not like I’m having panic attacks about it, but it’s just this constant, nagging feeling of embarrassment, you know? Well, that’s... that’s the tricky part to explain, isn't it? Because if you asked me right in that moment, I'd probably tell you I wanted to. Like, I'll think to myself, "Oh, I really want another sip of tea right now," or "I really want to go look at that poster on the wall." So in my head, it feels like a choice, like something I *want* to do. 

But then, if I really stop and think about it—and I have been thinking about it a lot lately, especially after Sarah snapped at me—it doesn't actually feel like a want at all. It feels more like... like a pressure building up inside me. It's almost like my body is humming, or like there's a motor running under my skin, and the only way to turn it off is to stand up. If I try to fight it, if I tell myself, "No, Margaret, you are going to sit here and listen to Mr. Harrison finish his point about the new grading rubric," the humming just gets louder. My legs start feeling restless, I start shifting in my chair, and my mind just completely detaches from whatever is being said because all I can focus on is how much I need to stand. 

So I guess... I guess it’s a bit of both? I mean, my brain gives me a reason to *want* to get up—like the coffee or the salt shaker—but underneath that, there's this overwhelming physical sensation that I *have* to get up. It’s like I’m tricking myself into thinking it’s a choice, just so I have an excuse to relieve that pressure. Does that make any sense at all? It sounds so strange when I say it out loud, but that's exactly how it feels.

Oh, no, no, it's not like that at all. It's not about preventing anything bad. I mean, I'm not sitting there thinking, "Oh, if I don't stand up right this second, the roof is going to cave in," or "If I don't go check the mail right now, something terrible will happen to my husband." If anything, the anxiety comes *after* I get up, because then I realize everyone is looking at me and I'm embarrassed! Like that time at Sarah's house, I wasn't anxious before I stood up to adjust the blinds, I just felt that urge to move. But the minute she snapped at me, oh, then I felt anxious and awful. So, no, getting up isn't a way to stop something bad from happening, and it's certainly not a way to calm my nerves. It's just... I just have to move.

Well, that’s just it, Doctor, I... I really don't think I can. And believe me, I have tried. I mean, that's exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place, this whole business of constantly getting up. I’ll go into these situations—like those faculty meetings with Mr. Harrison, or sitting down to a nice dinner party, or even just being at a restaurant with my husband—and I will tell myself, "Margaret, you are going to sit in this chair until the meal is over, or until the meeting is adjourned." I really, truly want to just stay seated like a normal person. 

But then, it just happens. I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I’ll feel this overwhelming urge to go refill the coffee pot, even if it’s only half empty, or I’ll decide I absolutely must walk to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board, or I'll jump up to get the salt shaker from the kitchen when there's already one on the table! And it's not like any of these things are urgent. Nobody is demanding more coffee right that second. But I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. 

I try to hold it in, I really do. I grip the armrests of my chair, or I fold my hands tightly in my lap, and I just try to will myself to stay put. But the longer I try to force it, the worse that humming feeling gets, until eventually, I just pop up out of my chair like a jack-in-the-box. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else. So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.

I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I just feel like I *have* to get up. I’ll convince myself I need to go refill my coffee—even if my mug is still half full—or I’ll pop up to check a stack of handouts on the side table, or sometimes I’ll just walk all the way to the back of the room and just stand there. \n\nAnd the thing is, none of it is ever really urgent. I mean, I could easily just stay in my chair like everybody else, but my brain finds these little excuses to leave my seat. Even at dinner, I'm constantly popping up to grab a salt shaker we don't really need, or to check on something in the kitchen. My husband just looks at me like, \"Can you please just sit and eat?\" and I'll look around and realize I'm the only one standing up again. It's just... I mean, it’s not like I’m having panic attacks about it, but it’s just this constant, nagging feeling of embarrassment, you know? It’s really starting to take a toll on my relationships, especially at work. Like, in those faculty meetings I mentioned, I can see my colleagues rolling their eyes or exchanging looks when I stand up for the third time in an hour. It was mortifying. \n\nAnd it’s not just at school, either. I’ve been part of this neighborhood book club for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We meet every other Tuesday, usually at Sarah’s house because she has that lovely sunroom. But lately, I just can’t seem to sit through the discussion. I’m always hopping up to get more tea, or to look at a book on her shelf, or to adjust the blinds. Last time, Sarah actually snapped at me and said, \"Could you please just light somewhere for five minutes so we can talk about the chapters?\" \n\nIt’s just... people are losing patience with me. Both at work and in my community group. I go to these things wanting to connect with people, wanting to be part of the team or the discussion, and instead, I leave feeling completely embarrassed and alienated. I just feel like I'm frustrating everyone around me, and I can't seem to stop doing it, even when I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to stay glued to my chair.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're getting up because you have to, or because you want to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... that’s the tricky part to explain, isn't it? Because if you asked me right in that moment, I'd probably tell you I wanted to. Like, I'll think to myself, \"Oh, I really want another sip of tea right now,\" or \"I really want to go look at that poster on the wall.\" So in my head, it feels like a choice, like something I *want* to do. \n\nBut then, if I really stop and think about it—and I have been thinking about it a lot lately, especially after Sarah snapped at me—it doesn't actually feel like a want at all. It feels more like... like a pressure building up inside me. It's almost like my body is humming, or like there's a motor running under my skin, and the only way to turn it off is to stand up. If I try to fight it, if I tell myself, \"No, Margaret, you are going to sit here and listen to Mr. Harrison finish his point about the new grading rubric,\" the humming just gets louder. My legs start feeling restless, I start shifting in my chair, and my mind just completely detaches from whatever is being said because all I can focus on is how much I need to stand. \n\nSo I guess... I guess it’s a bit of both? I mean, my brain gives me a reason to *want* to get up—like the coffee or the salt shaker—but underneath that, there's this overwhelming physical sensation that I *have* to get up. It’s like I’m tricking myself into thinking it’s a choice, just so I have an excuse to relieve that pressure. Does that make any sense at all? It sounds so strange when I say it out loud, but that's exactly how it feels.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up is something you do to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce anxiety?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, it's not like that at all. But what I'm feeling isn't like that. \n\nIt's really just... well, like I was saying, it's just that physical restlessness. It's not driven by fear or worry or some impending sense of doom. It's just my body wanting to move. If anything, the anxiety comes *after* I get up, because then I realize everyone is looking at me and I'm embarrassed! Like that time at Sarah's house, I wasn't anxious before I stood up to adjust the blinds, I just felt that urge to move. But the minute she snapped at me, oh, then I felt anxious and awful. So, no, getting up isn't a way to stop something bad from happening, and it's certainly not a way to calm my nerves. It's just... I just have to move.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you could stop getting up and stay seated if you really wanted to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s just it, Doctor, I... I really don't think I can. I’ll go into these situations—like those faculty meetings with Mr. Harrison, or sitting down to a nice dinner party, or even just being at a restaurant with my husband—and I will tell myself, \"Margaret, you are going to sit in this chair until the meal is over, or until the meeting is adjourned.\" I really, truly want to just stay seated like a normal person. \n\nBut then, it just happens. And it's not like any of these things are urgent. Nobody is demanding more coffee right that second. But I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. \n\nI try to hold it in, I really do. I grip the armrests of my chair, or I fold my hands tightly in my lap, and I just try to will myself to stay put. But the longer I try to force it, the worse that humming feeling gets, until eventually, I just pop up out of my chair like a jack-in-the-box. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else. So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Oh, no, not really. Honestly, that’s never been an issue for me. In fact, people are always quite surprised by how well I can focus, especially given how much I move around. Take my grading, for example. As a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly eleventh and twelfth graders, which means I am dealing with a mountain of essays every other week, let me tell you—you absolutely have to be able to zero in on what they're writing. And I can! I can set myself up at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a stack of thirty-five essays on the causes of the First World War, and my mind is completely on those papers. 

Now, I might be bouncing my heel up and down the entire time, or I might suddenly pop up to wipe down the kitchen counter after the fifth essay, exactly like we were just talking about with that... that humming feeling. But my attention on the actual task? It doesn't waver. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what the student was arguing in the previous paragraph, and I don't sit there staring at the page without taking anything in. 

Even going all the way back to when I was in graduate school, I never had trouble paying attention to the lectures or doing my research in the library. My husband, Richard, on the other hand, he's the one who gets distracted. He'll start fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet door, and then he'll wander off because he remembered he needed to check the tire pressure on the car, and three hours later the cabinet door is still hanging off its hinges! But me? No, if I'm engaged in an activity, my brain is right there with it. It's really just my body that wants to be somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention drifts at all. I can focus on things perfectly fine, it's just the staying glued to the chair while I do it that seems to be my cross to bear.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Habit? No, I wouldn't call it a habit at all. A habit is something you do without even realizing it, like tapping your fingers or, I don't know, putting your keys in the exact same dish every day without thinking. This isn't like that. It’s absolutely a compulsion. 

In fact, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, that is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. It's this dreadful pattern where I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is properly seated. I will just suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to do something—like I absolutely must refill the coffee right then and there, or I have to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout. And I know perfectly well that nothing is really urgent! The coffee isn't boiling over, and that handout has been on the bulletin board since Tuesday. But the feeling that I have to get up and do it... it’s so strong, it’s almost a physical pressure. 

I’ll look around at the other teachers at school, or our guests at the dinner table, and they are all just sitting there so calmly, eating or listening. And I just sit there willing myself to be like them, telling myself to just stay put, but that compulsion just builds and builds until I'm on my feet again making up some excuse about needing to stretch my legs or check on dessert. So yes, it is definitely a compulsion, not just a careless habit. I am very much aware of it happening, and I feel driven to do it, even when it makes absolutely no sense for the situation.

Impulse... yes. Yes, I suppose impulse is exactly the right word for it. It happens so quickly, you see. Like I was saying just a moment ago—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it truly is the entire reason I’m sitting in your office today, the very thing that brought me in—it’s this endless cycle of getting up during meetings or at dinner when every other person in the room is perfectly content to remain seated. 

It really is an impulse, because I certainly don't plan it! I don't sit down at a dinner party and think to myself, "In exactly fifteen minutes, I shall stand up." No, it just strikes me out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be sitting there, listening to a story or eating my salad, and suddenly the impulse hits that I absolutely must go refill the coffee pot. Or if I'm at school, sitting through one of Mr. Harrison's terribly dry faculty meetings, I'll get this sudden, impulsive urge to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board. 

And as I mentioned before, none of it is ever urgent! The coffee is fine, nobody is asking for a top-up, and that handout has been pinned to the board for days. But the impulse just flashes in my brain, and before I can even reason with myself—before I can even think, "Margaret, don't be ridiculous, just sit here and finish your meal"—I am already on my feet. My legs are pushing the chair back before my common sense can catch up. So, yes, it is highly impulsive. It’s like a spark just goes off, and I act on it instantly, even though it makes absolutely no sense to anyone else in the room.

Oh, goodness, yes. It goes back a very, very long way. You know, it’s funny you ask about when I was a child, because back then—especially for a young girl in the sixties—they didn't really know what to make of a little girl who couldn't just sit nicely with her hands folded in her lap. 

I remember my mother used to save all my old school records in this large, heavy accordion folder she kept in the hall closet. And if you looked at my report cards from elementary school, even as a very young girl, the teachers always wrote the exact same thing. They would write that I was a bright student, very capable, but that I simply could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. It was always, "Margaret is enthusiastic but needs to learn to remain seated," or "Margaret struggles to wait to be called upon." 

And my mother, bless her heart, she used to joke about it with her friends when they came over for coffee. She used to say that I must have worn a permanent path in the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! Because that was my favorite excuse, you see. I would constantly get up to sharpen my pencil just to have a reason to move my legs. I would grind those poor yellow pencils down to absolute nubs, just so I could justify standing up and walking to the front of the room again. So, yes, the restlessness was absolutely there, right from the very beginning. It’s just always been a part of how I operate, long before I was a teacher myself, back when I was just a little girl in pigtails trying to find an excuse to stretch my legs.

Oh, absolutely. It never really went away, it just... well, it just changed shape, I suppose you could say. Through high school and my university years, I was always the girl vibrating my knee under the library table. And even now—well, especially now, at my age, you'd think a sixty-year-old woman would have grown out of it, but I haven't in the slightest. 

Just to give you an idea of what it looks like today, when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays—and you know, as a secondary school teacher, the grading is simply endless, just mountains of papers every weekend—I will be sitting there trying to focus on a student's thesis statement, and I'll catch myself tapping my foot a mile a minute. Or clicking my pen. I use those retractable ballpoint pens, the blue ones, because I prefer the ink flow, but I will just click, click, click, over and over. Half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until my husband peeks his head into the study to ask what on earth that repetitive noise is. 

And it is not just at home or in my classroom, either. If I'm in church, sitting in those hard wooden pews during the sermon, it is a constant struggle. I am always shifting around. I cross one leg, then I cross the other, then I adjust my posture, then I'm tapping my foot again. I shift around so much that I literally have to have a stern internal conversation with myself. I have to actively remind myself to just settle down and be still so I don't distract the people sitting in the rows behind me. So, yes, the fidgeting has very much followed me right through my teenage years and straight into my adult life. It is just this constant, humming need to be moving some part of my body, even when I am supposed to be completely stationary.

I just feel like I'm frustrating everyone around me, and I can't seem to stop doing it, even when I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to stay glued to my chair.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're getting up because you have to, or because you want to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... that’s the tricky part to explain, isn't it? Because if you asked me right in that moment, I'd probably tell you I wanted to. Like, I'll think to myself, \"Oh, I really want another sip of tea right now,\" or \"I really want to go look at that poster on the wall.\" So in my head, it feels like a choice, like something I *want* to do. \n\nBut then, if I really stop and think about it—and I have been thinking about it a lot lately, especially after Sarah snapped at me—it doesn't actually feel like a want at all. It feels more like... like a pressure building up inside me. It's almost like my body is humming, or like there's a motor running under my skin, and the only way to turn it off is to stand up. If I try to fight it, if I tell myself, \"No, Margaret, you are going to sit here and listen to Mr. Harrison finish his point about the new grading rubric,\" the humming just gets louder. My legs start feeling restless, I start shifting in my chair, and my mind just completely detaches from whatever is being said because all I can focus on is how much I need to stand. \n\nSo I guess... I guess it’s a bit of both? I mean, my brain gives me a reason to *want* to get up—like the coffee or the salt shaker—but underneath that, there's this overwhelming physical sensation that I *have* to get up. It’s like I’m tricking myself into thinking it’s a choice, just so I have an excuse to relieve that pressure. Does that make any sense at all? It sounds so strange when I say it out loud, but that's exactly how it feels.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up is something you do to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce anxiety?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, it's not like that at all. It's not about preventing anything bad. I mean, I'm not sitting there thinking, \"Oh, if I don't stand up right this second, the roof is going to cave in,\" or \"If I don't go check the mail right now, something terrible will happen to my husband.\" It's nothing like that. And I wouldn't say it's to reduce anxiety, either. I mean, I know what anxiety feels like—my sister gets terrible anxiety, she used to have panic attacks right before she had to speak in public, just awful things where she couldn't breathe. But what I'm feeling isn't like that. \n\nIt's really just... well, like I was saying, it's just that physical restlessness. It's not driven by fear or worry or some impending sense of doom. It's just my body wanting to move. If anything, the anxiety comes *after* I get up, because then I realize everyone is looking at me and I'm embarrassed! Like that time at Sarah's house, I wasn't anxious before I stood up to adjust the blinds, I just felt that urge to move. But the minute she snapped at me, oh, then I felt anxious and awful. So, no, getting up isn't a way to stop something bad from happening, and it's certainly not a way to calm my nerves. It's just... I just have to move.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you could stop getting up and stay seated if you really wanted to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s just it, Doctor, I... I really don't think I can. And believe me, I have tried. I mean, that's exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place, this whole business of constantly getting up. I’ll go into these situations—like those faculty meetings with Mr. Harrison, or sitting down to a nice dinner party, or even just being at a restaurant with my husband—and I will tell myself, \"Margaret, you are going to sit in this chair until the meal is over, or until the meeting is adjourned.\" I really, truly want to just stay seated like a normal person. \n\nBut then, it just happens. I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I’ll feel this overwhelming urge to go refill the coffee pot, even if it’s only half empty, or I’ll decide I absolutely must walk to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board, or I'll jump up to get the salt shaker from the kitchen when there's already one on the table! And it's not like any of these things are urgent. Nobody is demanding more coffee right that second. But I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. \n\nI try to hold it in, I really do. I grip the armrests of my chair, or I fold my hands tightly in my lap, and I just try to will myself to stay put. But the longer I try to force it, the worse that humming feeling gets, until eventually, I just pop up out of my chair like a jack-in-the-box. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else. So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced difficulties with sustaining attention on tasks or activities throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, not really. Honestly, that’s never been an issue for me. In fact, people are always quite surprised by how well I can focus, especially given how much I move around. Take my grading, for example. As a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly eleventh and twelfth graders, which means I am dealing with a mountain of essays every other week, let me tell you—you absolutely have to be able to zero in on what they're writing. And I can! I can set myself up at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a stack of thirty-five essays on the causes of the First World War, and my mind is completely on those papers. \n\nNow, I might be bouncing my heel up and down the entire time, or I might suddenly pop up to wipe down the kitchen counter after the fifth essay, exactly like we were just talking about with that... that humming feeling. But my attention on the actual task? It doesn't waver. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what the student was arguing in the previous paragraph, and I don't sit there staring at the page without taking anything in. \n\nEven going all the way back to when I was in graduate school, I never had trouble paying attention to the lectures or doing my research in the library. My husband, Richard, on the other hand, he's the one who gets distracted. He'll start fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet door, and then he'll wander off because he remembered he needed to check the tire pressure on the car, and three hours later the cabinet door is still hanging off its hinges! But me? No, if I'm engaged in an activity, my brain is right there with it. It's really just my body that wants to be somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention drifts at all. I can focus on things perfectly fine, it's just the staying glued to the chair while I do it that seems to be my cross to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up and moving around is something you do out of habit, or is it something you feel compelled to do?\n\nPatient: Habit? No, I wouldn't call it a habit at all. A habit is something you do without even realizing it, like tapping your fingers or, I don't know, putting your keys in the exact same dish every day without thinking. This isn't like that. It’s absolutely a compulsion. \n\nIn fact, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, that is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. It's this dreadful pattern where I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is properly seated. I will just suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to do something—like I absolutely must refill the coffee right then and there, or I have to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout. And I know perfectly well that nothing is really urgent! The coffee isn't boiling over, and that handout has been on the bulletin board since Tuesday. But the feeling that I have to get up and do it... it’s so strong, it’s almost a physical pressure. \n\nI’ll look around at the other teachers at school, or our guests at the dinner table, and they are all just sitting there so calmly, eating or listening. And I just sit there willing myself to be like them, telling myself to just stay put, but that compulsion just builds and builds until I'm on my feet again making up some excuse about needing to stretch my legs or check on dessert. So yes, it is definitely a compulsion, not just a careless habit. I am very much aware of it happening, and I feel driven to do it, even when it makes absolutely no sense for the situation.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're acting on impulse when you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: Impulse... yes. Yes, I suppose impulse is exactly the right word for it. It happens so quickly, you see. Like I was saying just a moment ago—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it truly is the entire reason I’m sitting in your office today, the very thing that brought me in—it’s this endless cycle of getting up during meetings or at dinner when every other person in the room is perfectly content to remain seated. \n\nIt really is an impulse, because I certainly don't plan it! I don't sit down at a dinner party and think to myself, \"In exactly fifteen minutes, I shall stand up.\" No, it just strikes me out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be sitting there, listening to a story or eating my salad, and suddenly the impulse hits that I absolutely must go refill the coffee pot. Or if I'm at school, sitting through one of Mr. Harrison's terribly dry faculty meetings, I'll get this sudden, impulsive urge to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board. \n\nAnd as I mentioned before, none of it is ever urgent! The coffee is fine, nobody is asking for a top-up, and that handout has been pinned to the board for days. But the impulse just flashes in my brain, and before I can even reason with myself—before I can even think, \"Margaret, don't be ridiculous, just sit here and finish your meal\"—I am already on my feet. My legs are pushing the chair back before my common sense can catch up. So, yes, it is highly impulsive. It’s like a spark just goes off, and I act on it instantly, even though it makes absolutely no sense to anyone else in the room.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience a lot of fidgeting or restlessness when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. It goes back a very, very long way. You know, it’s funny you ask about when I was a child, because back then—especially for a young girl in the sixties—they didn't really know what to make of a little girl who couldn't just sit nicely with her hands folded in her lap. \n\nI remember my mother used to save all my old school records in this large, heavy accordion folder she kept in the hall closet. And if you looked at my report cards from elementary school, even as a very young girl, the teachers always wrote the exact same thing. They would write that I was a bright student, very capable, but that I simply could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. It was always, \"Margaret is enthusiastic but needs to learn to remain seated,\" or \"Margaret struggles to wait to be called upon.\" \n\nAnd my mother, bless her heart, she used to joke about it with her friends when they came over for coffee. She used to say that I must have worn a permanent path in the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! Because that was my favorite excuse, you see. I would constantly get up to sharpen my pencil just to have a reason to move my legs. I would grind those poor yellow pencils down to absolute nubs, just so I could justify standing up and walking to the front of the room again. So, yes, the restlessness was absolutely there, right from the very beginning. It’s just always been a part of how I operate, long before I was a teacher myself, back when I was just a little girl in pigtails trying to find an excuse to stretch my legs.\n\nDoctor: Did your restlessness and fidgeting continue into your teenage years and beyond?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It never really went away, it just... well, it just changed shape, I suppose you could say. Through high school and my university years, I was always the girl vibrating my knee under the library table. And even now—well, especially now, at my age, you'd think a sixty-year-old woman would have grown out of it, but I haven't in the slightest. \n\nJust to give you an idea of what it looks like today, when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays—and you know, as a secondary school teacher, the grading is simply endless, just mountains of papers every weekend—I will be sitting there trying to focus on a student's thesis statement, and I'll catch myself tapping my foot a mile a minute. Or clicking my pen. I use those retractable ballpoint pens, the blue ones, because I prefer the ink flow, but I will just click, click, click, over and over. Half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until my husband peeks his head into the study to ask what on earth that repetitive noise is. \n\nAnd it is not just at home or in my classroom, either. If I'm in church, sitting in those hard wooden pews during the sermon, it is a constant struggle. I am always shifting around. I cross one leg, then I cross the other, then I adjust my posture, then I'm tapping my foot again. I shift around so much that I literally have to have a stern internal conversation with myself. I have to actively remind myself to just settle down and be still so I don't distract the people sitting in the rows behind me. It is just this constant, humming need to be moving some part of my body, even when I am supposed to be completely stationary.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. Oh, goodness, no. No, I've never received any sort of official diagnosis for anything like that, not at all. You know, back when I was growing up, they didn't really have a name for this sort of thing, or if they did, they certainly weren't handing it out to little girls who just liked to sharpen their pencils too much. And it's not like any of these things are urgent. Nobody is demanding more coffee right that second. But I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. \n\nI try to hold it in, I really do. I grip the armrests of my chair, or I fold my hands tightly in my lap, and I just try to will myself to stay put. But the longer I try to force it, the worse that humming feeling gets, until eventually, I just pop up out of my chair like a jack-in-the-box. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else. So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced difficulties with sustaining attention on tasks or activities throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, not really. Honestly, that’s never been an issue for me. In fact, people are always quite surprised by how well I can focus, especially given how much I move around. Take my grading, for example. As a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly eleventh and twelfth graders, which means I am dealing with a mountain of essays every other week, let me tell you—you absolutely have to be able to zero in on what they're writing. And I can! I can set myself up at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a stack of thirty-five essays on the causes of the First World War, and my mind is completely on those papers. \n\nNow, I might be bouncing my heel up and down the entire time, or I might suddenly pop up to wipe down the kitchen counter after the fifth essay, exactly like we were just talking about with that... that humming feeling. But my attention on the actual task? It doesn't waver. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what the student was arguing in the previous paragraph, and I don't sit there staring at the page without taking anything in. \n\nEven going all the way back to when I was in graduate school, I never had trouble paying attention to the lectures or doing my research in the library. My husband, Richard, on the other hand, he's the one who gets distracted. He'll start fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet door, and then he'll wander off because he remembered he needed to check the tire pressure on the car, and three hours later the cabinet door is still hanging off its hinges! But me? No, if I'm engaged in an activity, my brain is right there with it. It's really just my body that wants to be somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention drifts at all. I can focus on things perfectly fine, it's just the staying glued to the chair while I do it that seems to be my cross to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up and moving around is something you do out of habit, or is it something you feel compelled to do?\n\nPatient: Habit? No, I wouldn't call it a habit at all. A habit is something you do without even realizing it, like tapping your fingers or, I don't know, putting your keys in the exact same dish every day without thinking. This isn't like that. It’s absolutely a compulsion. \n\nIn fact, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, that is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. It's this dreadful pattern where I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is properly seated. I will just suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to do something—like I absolutely must refill the coffee right then and there, or I have to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout. And I know perfectly well that nothing is really urgent! The coffee isn't boiling over, and that handout has been on the bulletin board since Tuesday. But the feeling that I have to get up and do it... it’s so strong, it’s almost a physical pressure. \n\nI’ll look around at the other teachers at school, or our guests at the dinner table, and they are all just sitting there so calmly, eating or listening. And I just sit there willing myself to be like them, telling myself to just stay put, but that compulsion just builds and builds until I'm on my feet again making up some excuse about needing to stretch my legs or check on dessert. So yes, it is definitely a compulsion, not just a careless habit. I am very much aware of it happening, and I feel driven to do it, even when it makes absolutely no sense for the situation.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're acting on impulse when you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: Impulse... yes. Yes, I suppose impulse is exactly the right word for it. It happens so quickly, you see. Like I was saying just a moment ago—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it truly is the entire reason I’m sitting in your office today, the very thing that brought me in—it’s this endless cycle of getting up during meetings or at dinner when every other person in the room is perfectly content to remain seated. \n\nIt really is an impulse, because I certainly don't plan it! I don't sit down at a dinner party and think to myself, \"In exactly fifteen minutes, I shall stand up.\" No, it just strikes me out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be sitting there, listening to a story or eating my salad, and suddenly the impulse hits that I absolutely must go refill the coffee pot. Or if I'm at school, sitting through one of Mr. Harrison's terribly dry faculty meetings, I'll get this sudden, impulsive urge to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board. \n\nAnd as I mentioned before, none of it is ever urgent! The coffee is fine, nobody is asking for a top-up, and that handout has been pinned to the board for days. But the impulse just flashes in my brain, and before I can even reason with myself—before I can even think, \"Margaret, don't be ridiculous, just sit here and finish your meal\"—I am already on my feet. My legs are pushing the chair back before my common sense can catch up. So, yes, it is highly impulsive. It’s like a spark just goes off, and I act on it instantly, even though it makes absolutely no sense to anyone else in the room.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience a lot of fidgeting or restlessness when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. It goes back a very, very long way. You know, it’s funny you ask about when I was a child, because back then—especially for a young girl in the sixties—they didn't really know what to make of a little girl who couldn't just sit nicely with her hands folded in her lap. \n\nI remember my mother used to save all my old school records in this large, heavy accordion folder she kept in the hall closet. And if you looked at my report cards from elementary school, even as a very young girl, the teachers always wrote the exact same thing. They would write that I was a bright student, very capable, but that I simply could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. It was always, \"Margaret is enthusiastic but needs to learn to remain seated,\" or \"Margaret struggles to wait to be called upon.\" \n\nAnd my mother, bless her heart, she used to joke about it with her friends when they came over for coffee. She used to say that I must have worn a permanent path in the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! Because that was my favorite excuse, you see. I would constantly get up to sharpen my pencil just to have a reason to move my legs. I would grind those poor yellow pencils down to absolute nubs, just so I could justify standing up and walking to the front of the room again. So, yes, the restlessness was absolutely there, right from the very beginning. It’s just always been a part of how I operate, long before I was a teacher myself, back when I was just a little girl in pigtails trying to find an excuse to stretch my legs.\n\nDoctor: Did your restlessness and fidgeting continue into your teenage years and beyond?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It never really went away, it just... well, it just changed shape, I suppose you could say. Through high school and my university years, I was always the girl vibrating my knee under the library table. And even now—well, especially now, at my age, you'd think a sixty-year-old woman would have grown out of it, but I haven't in the slightest. \n\nJust to give you an idea of what it looks like today, when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays—and you know, as a secondary school teacher, the grading is simply endless, just mountains of papers every weekend—I will be sitting there trying to focus on a student's thesis statement, and I'll catch myself tapping my foot a mile a minute. Or clicking my pen. I use those retractable ballpoint pens, the blue ones, because I prefer the ink flow, but I will just click, click, click, over and over. Half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until my husband peeks his head into the study to ask what on earth that repetitive noise is. \n\nAnd it is not just at home or in my classroom, either. If I'm in church, sitting in those hard wooden pews during the sermon, it is a constant struggle. I am always shifting around. I cross one leg, then I cross the other, then I adjust my posture, then I'm tapping my foot again. I shift around so much that I literally have to have a stern internal conversation with myself. I have to actively remind myself to just settle down and be still so I don't distract the people sitting in the rows behind me. So, yes, the fidgeting has very much followed me right through my teenage years and straight into my adult life. It is just this constant, humming need to be moving some part of my body, even when I am supposed to be completely stationary.\n\nDoctor: Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or experience symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions or making careless mistakes, in addition to your restlessness and fidgeting?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, no. No, I've never received any sort of official diagnosis for anything like that, not at all. Anyway, we’ll be discussing a chapter, and someone will be making a point, and before they’ve even finished their sentence, I’m already jumping in. I just can’t seem to help it! The response is already fully formed in my head, and it’s like it just pushes its way out of my mouth before my brain can tell my lips to wait their turn.

I’ll say, "Well, that won't work for the AP students," or "We tried that in 2018 and it was a disaster," right over the top of him. 

I always feel dreadful about it afterward, I really do. I don't mean to be rude or disrespectful, and I certainly don't want people to think I don't value their input. It’s just... it’s like the thought is a physical thing, and if I don't say it that exact second, I’ll burst. I just jump right in, completely unprompted, before they’ve even had a chance to put a period on the end of their sentence. It's terribly embarrassing, really, for a woman of my age and profession to struggle with simply letting another person finish speaking.

So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced difficulties with sustaining attention on tasks or activities throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, not really. Honestly, that’s never been an issue for me. In fact, people are always quite surprised by how well I can focus, especially given how much I move around. Take my grading, for example. As a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly eleventh and twelfth graders, which means I am dealing with a mountain of essays every other week, let me tell you—you absolutely have to be able to zero in on what they're writing. And I can! I can set myself up at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a stack of thirty-five essays on the causes of the First World War, and my mind is completely on those papers. \n\nNow, I might be bouncing my heel up and down the entire time, or I might suddenly pop up to wipe down the kitchen counter after the fifth essay, exactly like we were just talking about with that... that humming feeling. But my attention on the actual task? It doesn't waver. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what the student was arguing in the previous paragraph, and I don't sit there staring at the page without taking anything in. \n\nEven going all the way back to when I was in graduate school, I never had trouble paying attention to the lectures or doing my research in the library. My husband, Richard, on the other hand, he's the one who gets distracted. He'll start fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet door, and then he'll wander off because he remembered he needed to check the tire pressure on the car, and three hours later the cabinet door is still hanging off its hinges! But me? No, if I'm engaged in an activity, my brain is right there with it. It's really just my body that wants to be somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention drifts at all. I can focus on things perfectly fine, it's just the staying glued to the chair while I do it that seems to be my cross to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up and moving around is something you do out of habit, or is it something you feel compelled to do?\n\nPatient: Habit? No, I wouldn't call it a habit at all. A habit is something you do without even realizing it, like tapping your fingers or, I don't know, putting your keys in the exact same dish every day without thinking. This isn't like that. It’s absolutely a compulsion. \n\nIn fact, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, that is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. It's this dreadful pattern where I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is properly seated. I will just suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to do something—like I absolutely must refill the coffee right then and there, or I have to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout. And I know perfectly well that nothing is really urgent! The coffee isn't boiling over, and that handout has been on the bulletin board since Tuesday. But the feeling that I have to get up and do it... it’s so strong, it’s almost a physical pressure. \n\nI’ll look around at the other teachers at school, or our guests at the dinner table, and they are all just sitting there so calmly, eating or listening. And I just sit there willing myself to be like them, telling myself to just stay put, but that compulsion just builds and builds until I'm on my feet again making up some excuse about needing to stretch my legs or check on dessert. So yes, it is definitely a compulsion, not just a careless habit. I am very much aware of it happening, and I feel driven to do it, even when it makes absolutely no sense for the situation.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're acting on impulse when you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: Impulse... yes. Yes, I suppose impulse is exactly the right word for it. It happens so quickly, you see. Like I was saying just a moment ago—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it truly is the entire reason I’m sitting in your office today, the very thing that brought me in—it’s this endless cycle of getting up during meetings or at dinner when every other person in the room is perfectly content to remain seated. \n\nIt really is an impulse, because I certainly don't plan it! I don't sit down at a dinner party and think to myself, \"In exactly fifteen minutes, I shall stand up.\" No, it just strikes me out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be sitting there, listening to a story or eating my salad, and suddenly the impulse hits that I absolutely must go refill the coffee pot. Or if I'm at school, sitting through one of Mr. Harrison's terribly dry faculty meetings, I'll get this sudden, impulsive urge to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board. \n\nAnd as I mentioned before, none of it is ever urgent! The coffee is fine, nobody is asking for a top-up, and that handout has been pinned to the board for days. But the impulse just flashes in my brain, and before I can even reason with myself—before I can even think, \"Margaret, don't be ridiculous, just sit here and finish your meal\"—I am already on my feet. My legs are pushing the chair back before my common sense can catch up. So, yes, it is highly impulsive. It’s like a spark just goes off, and I act on it instantly, even though it makes absolutely no sense to anyone else in the room.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience a lot of fidgeting or restlessness when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. It goes back a very, very long way. You know, it’s funny you ask about when I was a child, because back then—especially for a young girl in the sixties—they didn't really know what to make of a little girl who couldn't just sit nicely with her hands folded in her lap. \n\nI remember my mother used to save all my old school records in this large, heavy accordion folder she kept in the hall closet. And if you looked at my report cards from elementary school, even as a very young girl, the teachers always wrote the exact same thing. They would write that I was a bright student, very capable, but that I simply could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. It was always, \"Margaret is enthusiastic but needs to learn to remain seated,\" or \"Margaret struggles to wait to be called upon.\" \n\nAnd my mother, bless her heart, she used to joke about it with her friends when they came over for coffee. She used to say that I must have worn a permanent path in the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! Because that was my favorite excuse, you see. I would constantly get up to sharpen my pencil just to have a reason to move my legs. I would grind those poor yellow pencils down to absolute nubs, just so I could justify standing up and walking to the front of the room again. So, yes, the restlessness was absolutely there, right from the very beginning. It’s just always been a part of how I operate, long before I was a teacher myself, back when I was just a little girl in pigtails trying to find an excuse to stretch my legs.\n\nDoctor: Did your restlessness and fidgeting continue into your teenage years and beyond?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It never really went away, it just... well, it just changed shape, I suppose you could say. Through high school and my university years, I was always the girl vibrating my knee under the library table. And even now—well, especially now, at my age, you'd think a sixty-year-old woman would have grown out of it, but I haven't in the slightest. \n\nJust to give you an idea of what it looks like today, when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays—and you know, as a secondary school teacher, the grading is simply endless, just mountains of papers every weekend—I will be sitting there trying to focus on a student's thesis statement, and I'll catch myself tapping my foot a mile a minute. Or clicking my pen. I use those retractable ballpoint pens, the blue ones, because I prefer the ink flow, but I will just click, click, click, over and over. Half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until my husband peeks his head into the study to ask what on earth that repetitive noise is. \n\nAnd it is not just at home or in my classroom, either. If I'm in church, sitting in those hard wooden pews during the sermon, it is a constant struggle. I am always shifting around. I cross one leg, then I cross the other, then I adjust my posture, then I'm tapping my foot again. I shift around so much that I literally have to have a stern internal conversation with myself. I have to actively remind myself to just settle down and be still so I don't distract the people sitting in the rows behind me. So, yes, the fidgeting has very much followed me right through my teenage years and straight into my adult life. It is just this constant, humming need to be moving some part of my body, even when I am supposed to be completely stationary.\n\nDoctor: Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or experience symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions or making careless mistakes, in addition to your restlessness and fidgeting?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, no. No, I've never received any sort of official diagnosis for anything like that, not at all. You know, back when I was growing up, they didn't really have a name for this sort of thing, or if they did, they certainly weren't handing it out to little girls who just liked to sharpen their pencils too much. And as for the other things you mentioned—the inattention, the careless mistakes, not following instructions—no, that really hasn't been my experience. \n\nIn fact, I've always prided myself on being quite the opposite when it comes to the details! As a teacher, you simply have to be. I mean, if I couldn't follow instructions or if I was constantly making careless errors, I'd never survive grading those mountains of essays I told you about. I can spot a dangling modifier or an improperly formatted bibliography from a mile away! I'm actually very meticulous, very organized. I have my lesson plans mapped out weeks in advance, color-coded and everything. \n\nIt's never been a problem of my mind drifting away or forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing. My mind is always very sharp, very engaged. It's just the physical part, you see—the body. The body is always humming, always needing to move, even when the brain is perfectly focused on the task at hand. So, no, I wouldn't say I struggle with inattention or making mistakes at all. It's really just the restlessness, the inability to stay put when everyone else seems so perfectly content to just sit there.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever acted on impulses without fully thinking them through in situations beyond just getting up and moving around?\n\nPatient: Oh, my, yes. Yes, I suppose I do, now that you mention it. It’s not just the moving around, no. It’s... well, it’s my mouth, too, to be perfectly honest. I have a terrible habit of just blurting things out. \n\nIt happens all the time in group discussions. You know, I’m part of this wonderful book club—we meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually at Susan’s house because she has that lovely sunroom, though occasionally we rotate. Anyway, we’ll be discussing a chapter, and someone will be making a point, and before they’ve even finished their sentence, I’m already jumping in. I just can’t seem to help it! The response is already fully formed in my head, and it’s like it just pushes its way out of my mouth before my brain can tell my lips to wait their turn. \n\nAnd it’s not just at book club, either. I’ll say, \"Well, that won't work for the AP students,\" or \"We tried that in 2018 and it was a disaster,\" right over the top of him. \n\nI always feel dreadful about it afterward, I really do. I don't mean to be rude or disrespectful, and I certainly don't want people to think I don't value their input. It’s just... it’s like the thought is a physical thing, and if I don't say it that exact second, I’ll burst. I go to these things wanting to connect with people, wanting to be part of the team or the discussion, and instead, I leave feeling completely embarrassed and alienated. I just feel like I'm frustrating everyone around me, and I can't seem to stop doing it, even when I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to stay glued to my chair.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're getting up because you have to, or because you want to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... that’s the tricky part to explain, isn't it? Because if you asked me right in that moment, I'd probably tell you I wanted to. Like, I'll think to myself, \"Oh, I really want another sip of tea right now,\" or \"I really want to go look at that poster on the wall.\" So in my head, it feels like a choice, like something I *want* to do. \n\nBut then, if I really stop and think about it—and I have been thinking about it a lot lately, especially after Sarah snapped at me—it doesn't actually feel like a want at all. It feels more like... like a pressure building up inside me. It's almost like my body is humming, or like there's a motor running under my skin, and the only way to turn it off is to stand up. If I try to fight it, if I tell myself, \"No, Margaret, you are going to sit here and listen to Mr. Harrison finish his point about the new grading rubric,\" the humming just gets louder. My legs start feeling restless, I start shifting in my chair, and my mind just completely detaches from whatever is being said because all I can focus on is how much I need to stand. \n\nSo I guess... I guess it’s a bit of both? I mean, my brain gives me a reason to *want* to get up—like the coffee or the salt shaker—but underneath that, there's this overwhelming physical sensation that I *have* to get up. It’s like I’m tricking myself into thinking it’s a choice, just so I have an excuse to relieve that pressure. Does that make any sense at all? It sounds so strange when I say it out loud, but that's exactly how it feels.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up is something you do to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce anxiety?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, it's not like that at all. It's not about preventing anything bad. I mean, I'm not sitting there thinking, \"Oh, if I don't stand up right this second, the roof is going to cave in,\" or \"If I don't go check the mail right now, something terrible will happen to my husband.\" It's nothing like that. And I wouldn't say it's to reduce anxiety, either. I mean, I know what anxiety feels like—my sister gets terrible anxiety, she used to have panic attacks right before she had to speak in public, just awful things where she couldn't breathe. But what I'm feeling isn't like that. \n\nIt's really just... well, like I was saying, it's just that physical restlessness. It's not driven by fear or worry or some impending sense of doom. It's just my body wanting to move. If anything, the anxiety comes *after* I get up, because then I realize everyone is looking at me and I'm embarrassed! Like that time at Sarah's house, I wasn't anxious before I stood up to adjust the blinds, I just felt that urge to move. But the minute she snapped at me, oh, then I felt anxious and awful. So, no, getting up isn't a way to stop something bad from happening, and it's certainly not a way to calm my nerves. It's just... I just have to move.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you could stop getting up and stay seated if you really wanted to?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s just it, Doctor, I... I really don't think I can. And believe me, I have tried. I mean, that's exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place, this whole business of constantly getting up. I’ll go into these situations—like those faculty meetings with Mr. Harrison, or sitting down to a nice dinner party, or even just being at a restaurant with my husband—and I will tell myself, \"Margaret, you are going to sit in this chair until the meal is over, or until the meeting is adjourned.\" I really, truly want to just stay seated like a normal person. \n\nBut then, it just happens. I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I’ll feel this overwhelming urge to go refill the coffee pot, even if it’s only half empty, or I’ll decide I absolutely must walk to the back of the room to check a handout on the bulletin board, or I'll jump up to get the salt shaker from the kitchen when there's already one on the table! And it's not like any of these things are urgent. Nobody is demanding more coffee right that second. But I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. \n\nI try to hold it in, I really do. I grip the armrests of my chair, or I fold my hands tightly in my lap, and I just try to will myself to stay put. But the longer I try to force it, the worse that humming feeling gets, until eventually, I just pop up out of my chair like a jack-in-the-box. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else. So, to answer your question, no... no, I don't think I can just stop if I want to, because I *do* want to, and I still can't.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced difficulties with sustaining attention on tasks or activities throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, not really. Honestly, that’s never been an issue for me. In fact, people are always quite surprised by how well I can focus, especially given how much I move around. Take my grading, for example. As a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly eleventh and twelfth graders, which means I am dealing with a mountain of essays every other week, let me tell you—you absolutely have to be able to zero in on what they're writing. And I can! I can set myself up at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a stack of thirty-five essays on the causes of the First World War, and my mind is completely on those papers. \n\nNow, I might be bouncing my heel up and down the entire time, or I might suddenly pop up to wipe down the kitchen counter after the fifth essay, exactly like we were just talking about with that... that humming feeling. But my attention on the actual task? It doesn't waver. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what the student was arguing in the previous paragraph, and I don't sit there staring at the page without taking anything in. \n\nEven going all the way back to when I was in graduate school, I never had trouble paying attention to the lectures or doing my research in the library. My husband, Richard, on the other hand, he's the one who gets distracted. He'll start fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet door, and then he'll wander off because he remembered he needed to check the tire pressure on the car, and three hours later the cabinet door is still hanging off its hinges! But me? No, if I'm engaged in an activity, my brain is right there with it. It's really just my body that wants to be somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention drifts at all. I can focus on things perfectly fine, it's just the staying glued to the chair while I do it that seems to be my cross to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like getting up and moving around is something you do out of habit, or is it something you feel compelled to do?\n\nPatient: Habit? No, I wouldn't call it a habit at all. A habit is something you do without even realizing it, like tapping your fingers or, I don't know, putting your keys in the exact same dish every day without thinking. This isn't like that. It’s absolutely a compulsion. \n\nIn fact, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, that is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. I will just suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to do something—like I absolutely must refill the coffee right then and there, or I have to walk all the way to the back of the room to check a handout. And I know perfectly well that nothing is really urgent! The coffee isn't boiling over, and that handout has been on the bulletin board since Tuesday. But the feeling that I have to get up and do it... it’s so strong, it’s almost a physical pressure. \n\nI’ll look around at the other teachers at school, or our guests at the dinner table, and they are all just sitting there so calmly, eating or listening. So yes, it is definitely a compulsion, not just a careless habit. I don't sit down at a dinner party and think to myself, \"In exactly fifteen minutes, I shall stand up.\" No, it just strikes me out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be sitting there, listening to a story or eating my salad, and suddenly the impulse hits that I absolutely must go refill the coffee pot. It’s like a spark just goes off, and I act on it instantly, even though it makes absolutely no sense to anyone else in the room.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience a lot of fidgeting or restlessness when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. It goes back a very, very long way. You know, it’s funny you ask about when I was a child, because back then—especially for a young girl in the sixties—they didn't really know what to make of a little girl who couldn't just sit nicely with her hands folded in her lap. \n\nI remember my mother used to save all my old school records in this large, heavy accordion folder she kept in the hall closet. Well, that is an interesting question, because... well, I suppose if I really think back, I’ve always been a bit of a doer, you know? Now, it’s just me in this quiet house, and without all that external chaos to manage, this internal restlessness has just amplified. It feels more like... like a pressure building up inside me. It's almost like my body is humming, or like there's a motor running under my skin, and the only way to turn it off is to stand up. Like that time at Sarah's house, I wasn't anxious before I stood up to adjust the blinds, I just felt that urge to move. But the minute she snapped at me, oh, then I felt anxious and awful. Well, goodness, as a child? That’s going back quite a ways, isn't it? Let me think. You know, I really don't believe I did. I mean, you have to remember the era I grew up in. This was the late sixties and early seventies, and my mother was very, very particular about how young ladies were supposed to conduct themselves. We lived in this lovely, rather formal two-story colonial on Elm Street—my father was a bank manager, you see, so appearances were simply everything to them. There was absolutely no tolerance for running through the house or climbing on the furniture, or really any sort of roughhousing at all. 

I certainly wasn't out scaling trees in the neighborhood or tearing through the yard like a hooligan. I spent a lot of time doing quiet activities, or at least, activities that were deemed appropriate for a girl my age. I took piano lessons for eight years with Mrs. Gable down the street, which required an agonizing amount of sitting still on this terribly hard wooden bench, and I helped my mother in the kitchen, shelling peas or snapping green beans for Sunday dinners. I suppose I was always busy, always doing something with my hands, but as for excessive running around or climbing on things? No, no, I really don't think so. 

I just don't have any memories of being that kind of wildly physical child. Honestly, if I had even tried to climb the big oak tree in our front yard, my mother would have had my hide! She used to put me in these stiff, itchy dresses with the little white tights, and the primary goal of my day was simply not to ruin the tights. So, no, I can't say I experienced anything like that back then. It really is just this current situation... this recent, awful inability to just stay in my chair at the school or at Susan's house that has me so turned around. ADHD? Oh, heavens no. No one has ever mentioned anything like that to me. I mean, when I think of ADHD, I think of the little boys in my seventh-grade history classes—the ones who can't stop tapping their pencils on the desk, or who blurt out answers before I've even finished asking the question, or who are practically bouncing out of their seats to go to the pencil sharpener for the fourth time in a single period. Well, stress or pressure... let me think about that. You know, it’s hard to say if it’s worse under stress because, quite frankly, teaching middle school is practically the definition of stress! But... no, I wouldn't say the stress changes the impulses themselves. 

I mean, take last month, for example. We had the state evaluations coming up, which is always a terribly tense time. So, whether I’m under a mountain of pressure with the school board, or just having a lovely, quiet Sunday morning at home with absolutely nothing on my agenda... the feeling is exactly the same. The urge to get up and find something to do doesn't seem to care whether I'm stressed or relaxed. It just... happens, regardless of what's going on around me or how much pressure I'm under. It's terribly frustrating, really, because if it were just stress, I could at least try to manage that, couldn't I? I could take up yoga or deep breathing or something. It’s like my body overrides my brain, no matter how much I genuinely want to just sit still and participate like everyone else.
